transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-10 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Janelle Ortiz (CTO, BlueArc), Ravi Menon (Platform Eng), Priya Kumar (PM)

[00:00] Sofia Patel: Hey, thanks all for joining, this is Sofia from Redwood, Marcus is our performance SE. Today we want to focus on guardrails — operational placement of your safety filters and what they do to latency/throughput, esp in a healthcare workflow.

[00:30] Janelle Ortiz: Thanks, yeah we have a hard latency budget — med-summaries should be under 400ms ideally, P90. Also big question: can we send patient text to an external moderation API or does everything need to stay in our VPC?

[01:05] Marcus Lee: quick answer, it depends. If you need full on-prem then moderation has to live inside your private deployment — which is feasible but changes trade-offs. If hosted, we can route to a managed moderation service, but that adds network RTT. We'll walk numbers.

[03:10] Ravi Menon: and what about streaming? We stream partials into the UI — moderation blocking that stream is a problem for UX.

[05:00] Marcus Lee: Right. There are three common placements we discussed:
- pre-filter (classify the prompt on CPU before sending to model) — very fast, avoids wasted generations for disallowed input, but only input-level check so it misses generation-time toxicity;
- inline (safety model runs on the same GPU process during or between token generation steps) — more accurate for generation-time issues, but increases per-token latency and complexity;
- post-filter async (generate first, then run a classifier async and redact or rollback) — lowest impact on generation latency but adds end-to-end time for a final verified response, and tricky if you need to block release.

[08:15] Priya Kumar: Could you put estimated latencies on those? ballpark P90 overheads?

[12:20] Marcus Lee: Sure — ballparks from our internal tests (your mileage varies with model size and infra):
- pre-filter (light classifier on CPU/int8): ~= 8–30ms per request extra, negligible throughput impact, scales well with many small VMs.
- inline (same GPU): token-level checks add ~10–60ms per token unless you batch safety model generations; for long generations this multiplies and can push P90 over budget — worst-case when safety runs synchronously after each chunk.
- post-filter async (dedicated CPU or separate GPU): adds 50–250ms end-to-end depending on model, but doesn't increase per-token latency so streaming looks normal until you block final commit.
He adds: these numbers assume optimized quantized classifiers and a sane tokenization strategy.

[16:40] Janelle Ortiz: So for our 400ms P90 we probably want pre-filter plus fast heuristics for streaming and then a background async post-filter for final audit?

[21:00] Marcus Lee: That's the common pattern. Pre-filter to catch obvious violations using cheap N-gram heuristics + small classifier (int8). Then if generation passes, allow streaming. Meanwhile run a more expensive context-aware safety check async and flag items in audit logs. If post-filter fails, you can either revoke content or mark for human review.

[26:30] Sofia Patel: A big topic we found is KV cache interactions. If you cache generations or prefix tokens, you might cache responses that later would have been blocked by a new safety rule or a changed classifier. So you need to version cache keys by the safety policy hash.

[32:10] Ravi Menon: Oof, versioning the KV cache seems like it could blow cache hit rates. Any best practices?

[36:00] Marcus Lee: A few patterns:
- include the safety-policy-id or safety-model-checksum in the cache key but keep it separate from the main content key;
- cache moderation verdicts separately: if same user prompt seen before, short-circuit with cached verdict;
- for streaming you can cache intermediate KV slots but keep final content validation step uncached until post-filter passes;
- use TTLs aggressively for safety-related cache entries so policy churn doesn't poison long-lived caches.
He stumbles a bit: "we saw hit rates drop by 12% when we naively included policy version — but separate verdict cache kept overall latency good."

[40:15] Priya Kumar: What about batching? If you batch N requests to improve throughput on Dedicated GPUs, how do safety checks interact?

[44:30] Marcus Lee: Batching is tricky. If safety is inline per request you either run safety per item in the batch (adds cost N times) or you run a single batch safety pass which may be faster but increases tail latency if one item is slower. For streaming clients batching can increase per-client latency due to aggregation windows. Recommendation: configure batching windows with low max delay for interactive flows (e.g., 5–15ms) and prefer pre-filtering so most disallowed inputs don't enter batches. For heavy throughput endpoints (e.g., nightly job) batching with separate safety pass is fine.

[47:50] Janelle Ortiz: ok this was super helpful. We need the microbenchmarks to make a decision on inline vs async. If we cannot leave the VPC, then we need on-prem options for the safety model — can Redwood package that?

[48:20] Sofia Patel: Yes for private deployments we can ship the safety classifier as part of the private bundle — quantized int8 versions to run on CPU or on smaller GPU. We'll include deployment options in the security doc.

[48:40] Marcus Lee: final notes: heuristics to short-circuit (regex, denylist) are cheap and very effective as a first line. For higher recall we recommend a small quantized safety model on CPU + async more powerful model for audits. Also consider user-level caching of allowed responses and TTL for verdicts. We'll provide benchmark configs: (A) pre-filter CPU int8 + cached verdicts, (B) inline GPU safety (quantized) with per-token checks, (C) generate-then-async post-filter. Marcus: I'll run microbenchmarks in staging and share numbers, and we'll add specific P90/P99 targets to the spreadsheet.

[49:10] Sofia Patel: Great, we'll also attach the security checklist, SOC2/ISO notes and KMS integration options, and the benchmark spreadsheet (link). Any questions?

[49:30] Priya Kumar: nope, thanks.

[49:45] Janelle Ortiz: thanks all, talk soon.

Notes: transcription contains some mis-hearings ("K-V cash" occasionally), occasional speaker label drift. Shared artifacts: benchmark spreadsheet (link: drive.redwood/benchmarks/BAH-moderation), security checklist (link: drive.redwood/security/BAH-checklist).
